items.quote: the man of God is buried; lay my bones beside his bones. For the message he declared by the word of the Lord against the altar in Bethel and against all the shrines on the high places in the towns of Samaria will certainly come true.
items.contrast: The man of God originally declared the message, whereas the speaker tells his sons that it will come true.
items.reason: The speaker is a plausible answer because he is the one now saying the message will come true. The generic verb “gives” and the pronoun “he” blur that role with the man of God’s role as the original declarer. Asking who originally declared the message would make the key unique.

items.quote: A son named Josiah will be born to the house of David. On you he will sacrifice the priests of the high places who make offerings here
items.contrast: The future son Josiah is the actor in the prophecy, not Jeroboam, who is merely standing by the altar when it is announced.
items.reason: Jeroboam is a plausible misreading because he is present at the altar, but the prophecy introduces Josiah and then says that “he” will sacrifice the priests. In this context, sacrificing them entails killing them.

items.quote: The total number of family leaders over the fighting men was 2,600. Under their command was an army of 307,500 men trained for war
items.contrast: The 2,600 family leaders command the army, while Jeiel and Maaseiah are involved in mustering it.
items.reason: Jeiel and Maaseiah are plausible because they are named in connection with organizing the army. The explicit phrase “Under their command,” however, refers to the immediately preceding 2,600 family leaders.

items.quote: “You will see it with your own eyes,” answered Elisha, “but you will not eat any of it!”
items.contrast: The low-price prophecy comes before the officer’s doubt; Elisha’s reply to that doubt is that the officer will see the fulfillment but not eat any of it.
items.reason: The market prices are a plausible answer because Elisha declares them in the opening speech, but they prompt rather than answer the doubt. The passage explicitly marks the see-but-not-eat statement as Elisha’s answer.

items.quote: took Joash son of Ahaziah and stole him away from among the royal princes, who were about to be murdered. She put him and his nurse in a bedroom to hide him from Athaliah; so he was not killed. He remained hidden with his nurse at the temple of the Lord for six years
items.contrast: Joash, Ahaziah’s surviving son, remains hidden with the nurse; Ahaziah himself is already dead.
items.reason: Ahaziah is a plausible misreading because the question names him possessively, but the opening establishes that he is dead. Joash is then named as his son, and the subsequent pronouns identify Joash as the person hidden with his nurse.
